item.title: PACIFIC Polytechnic’s defamation proceedings against Opposition MP
item.description: PACIFIC Polytechnic’s defamation proceedings against Opposition MP Alvick Maharaj will return to the High Court in Suva on September 22 for a pre-trial conference. The matter was called yesterday before Master Vandhana Lal in the High Court, with Mr Maharaj represented by Jitendra Reddy Lawyers.
item.content:encoded:
PACIFIC Polytechnic’s defamation proceedings against Opposition MP Alvick Maharaj will return to the High Court in Suva on September 22 for a pre-trial conference.

The matter was called yesterday before Master Vandhana Lal in the High Court, with Mr Maharaj represented by Jitendra Reddy Lawyers.

Pacific Polytechnic filed the proceedings against Mr Maharaj on April 10, 2026, claiming damages over alleged defamatory statements he made and circulated publicly.

In its statement of claim, the institution alleges Mr Maharaj issued a media statement on January 14 titled “Call for Urgent Investigation into Pacific Polytech Following Leaked Salary Crisis and Financial Mismanagement Allegations”.

The statement was allegedly circulated through social media, the Parliamentary Opposition Chambers page and local media.

The institution claims the publication contained false and malicious imputations that it was operating unlawfully, mismanaging public funds, facing financial instability and improperly withholding staff salaries.

Pacific Polytechnic also alleges Mr Maharaj relied on a Standing Committee on Social Affairs report that Parliament had withdrawn.

The claim further alleges defamatory remarks were made against the institution’s chairperson, Dr Ganeshwar Chand.

A cease-and-desist notice was issued to Mr Maharaj on January 27, requesting that the posts be removed, a public apology issued and an undertaking given

The institution claims the requests were not complied with.

It is seeking general, punitive, and exemplary damages, interest and legal costs.

The writ was served on Mr Maharaj at the Parliament complex on April 14.

The court has yet to determine the allegations.

item.title: Court rejects Saneem as witness in Prof Biman Prasad trial
item.description: The Suva Magistrates Court has rejected the prosecution’s application to produce former Registrar of Political Parties Mohammed Saneem as a witness in the trial of former deputy Prime Minister Professor Biman Prasad. Magistrate Yogesh Prasad, however, ruled that a certified true copy of the disputed document could be admitted into evidence.
item.content:encoded:
The Suva Magistrates Court has rejected the prosecution’s application to produce former Registrar of Political Parties Mohammed Saneem as a witness in the trial of former deputy Prime Minister Professor Biman Prasad.

Magistrate Yogesh Prasad, however, ruled that a certified true copy of the disputed document could be admitted into evidence.

Meanwhile, Magistrate Prasad has directed the prosecution to clarify the source of witness statements it intends to rely on in the trial.

Magistrate Prasad made the direction after defence lawyer Richard Naidu raised concerns about four witness statements disclosed during the trial, with two originating from an earlier investigation file and two from the current prosecution file.

Mr Naidu argued that if the prosecution intended to rely on material taken from another investigation file, it would have an obligation to disclose all relevant material from that file.

The Magistrate directed the relevant investigator to be present when the matter resumes at 2.30pm so the court could establish the facts surrounding the two files and the witness statements.

He said he did not want further submissions from parties at that stage without the necessary factual information.

The prosecution indicated it would proceed with the material already disclosed to the defence and that the investigator could be questioned during the trial if necessary.

item.title: Election funding concerns
item.description: VOTERS could be left in the dark about who is financing political parties under proposed changes to Fiji’s political donation laws. Transparency and Integrity Fiji (TIF) program officer Tarusila Reniu said the proposed changes could create opportunities for ‘dark money’ influence, foreign interference and elite capture in domestic elections.
item.content:encoded:
VOTERS could be left in the dark about who is financing political parties under proposed changes to Fiji’s political donation laws.

Transparency and Integrity Fiji (TIF) program officer Tarusila Reniu said the proposed changes could create opportunities for ‘dark money’ influence, foreign interference and elite capture in domestic elections.

Ms Reniu made the submission to the Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights as it considers four election-related bills before Parliament.

“Bill 31, Clause 8 of the Political Party Act would remove existing limits on political donations and allow contributions from non-citizens and former Fiji citizens, provided they were declared within 60 days of polling day,” she said.

Ms Reniu said the 60-day disclosure period meant voters would cast their ballots without knowing which external or wealthy entities were financing candidates or political parties.

“This could allow donors to use financial backing to influence public policy or seek favourable treatment in administrative decisions.”

Ms Reniu also said post-poll disclosure would significantly reduce the ability of the media and civil society organisations such as TIF to scrutinise political funding before an election.

TIF has recommended reinstating strict caps on political donations and maintaining a total prohibition on foreign or non-citizen financing of political parties.

“However, if foreign or non-citizen contributions were allowed under a revised framework, Parliament should establish a real-time, searchable digital public registry of donors.”

She also called for comprehensive conflict-of-interest declarations for all candidates and elected officials.

Ms Reniu said any breach, non-declaration or omission involving foreign funding should automatically be referred to the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption for prosecution under anti-corruption laws, including the Prevention of Bribery Act.

item.title: Polling day ‘could become campaign day’
item.description: POLLING day could become another campaign day if political parties are allowed to provide voters with free transport, food or refreshments under the Electoral (Amendment) Bill 2026. Centre for Democracy and Dialogue (CDD) chief executive Nilesh Lal described Clause 26 as one of the most problematic provisions in the Bill and recommended it be deleted.
item.content:encoded:
POLLING day could become another campaign day if political parties are allowed to provide voters with free transport, food or refreshments under the Electoral (Amendment) Bill 2026.

Centre for Democracy and Dialogue (CDD) chief executive Nilesh Lal described Clause 26 as one of the most problematic provisions in the Bill and recommended it be deleted.

Clause 26 would amend Section 114 of the Electoral Act to allow political parties, candidates or their representatives to provide free transportation to and from polling venues, as well as food and refreshments, provided they do not influence or attempt to influence a person’s vote.

Mr Lal said accessibility to polling stations was not an issue that justified the proposal, with existing provisions requiring voters to be assigned to polling stations within reasonable walking distance of their residences.

“The Supervisor of Elections had previously indicated that efforts were made to establish polling stations within 500 metres of voters’ residences,” he said.

He said more than 2000 polling stations operated on election day and polling venues met or exceeded international accessibility standards.

Mr Lal said free transport and food could create opportunities for undue influence, as influence could arise through gratitude, social obligation or interaction with party workers.

He said where transport assistance was genuinely required, it should be provided by election authorities rather than political parties.

“The underlying democratic principle is fairly straightforward. You need to keep material benefits separate from the act of voting.”

item.title: Court reserves ruling on late evidence in Biman Prasad trial
item.description: The Suva Magistrates Court has reserved its ruling until tomorrow on whether the prosecution can rely on a newly disclosed witness statement and certified company documents in the trial of former deputy Prime Minister Professor Biman Prasad. Magistrate Yogesh Prasad said he would need to consider the competing submissions, particularly the accused’s constitutional right to a fair trial, after the
item.content:encoded:
The Suva Magistrates Court has reserved its ruling until tomorrow on whether the prosecution can rely on a newly disclosed witness statement and certified company documents in the trial of former deputy Prime Minister Professor Biman Prasad.

Magistrate Yogesh Prasad said he would need to consider the competing submissions, particularly the accused’s constitutional right to a fair trial, after the prosecution disclosed the material during the course of the trial.

Manager Legal Joseph Work argued that its duty to disclose relevant material was continuing and relied on several authorities, including Supreme Court decisions, to submit that late disclosure did not automatically amount to prejudice.

Mr Work submitted that the additional disclosure comprised a statement from former Registrar of Political Parties Mohammed Saneem and a certified copy of a company document.

He said Mr Saneem’s statement contained no new material that would prejudice the defence and that the evidence was substantially similar to evidence already disclosed.

Defence lawyer Richard Naidu, however, argued that the introduction of Mr Saneem as a new witness at this stage created a real disadvantage because defence would need time to investigate the witness, his background and the relevance of his evidence.

Mr Naidu also submitted that any adjournment to allow the defence to prepare would itself cause further delay and affect Professor Prasad’s constitutional right to have his trial concluded without unreasonable delay.

Magistrate Prasad questioned the prosecution about the timing of the new evidence and acknowledged that, while the prosecution had a continuing duty of disclosure, the court also had to consider the accused’s constitutional rights.

He noted that a new witness constituted new evidence, even if the witness was expected to give evidence on substantially the same matters as another witness.

Mr Work maintained there had been no bad faith and that the statement was disclosed after it was recorded.

He also argued that the defence would have an opportunity to cross-examine Mr Saneem if the witness was permitted to give evidence.

Mr Naidu disputed that the issue could simply be resolved by an adjournment, arguing that repeated delays had already affected the progress of the trial and the availability of defence.

He also submitted that the prosecution should have sought the court’s directions before introducing further material once the trial was under way.

Magistrate Prasad said that going forward, any further new material introduced during the trial would require the prosecution to seek the court’s leave before it could be admitted.

The ruling will be delivered at 11.30am tomorrow, after which the court will determine how the trial proceeds.

item.title: Union wants payroll failures investigated
item.description: THE Fiji Teachers Union is calling for greater accountability and transparency over failures in the Ministry of Education’s human resources and payroll systems. FTU general secretary Muniappa Goundar said yesterday an independent review or inquiry should be considered if necessary to establish how the failures occurred.
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Teachers Union is calling for greater accountability and transparency over failures in the Ministry of Education’s human resources and payroll systems.

FTU general secretary Muniappa Goundar said yesterday an independent review or inquiry should be considered if necessary to establish how the failures occurred.

“We would support an independent review or inquiry if it is necessary to establish how these failures occurred, particularly where public funds were paid to people who were no longer employed while legitimate teachers have had their salaries stopped,” he said.

Mr Goundar said the purpose of any review should not be to target individual officers but to identify weaknesses in the systems and prevent similar failures from happening again.

He said administrative problems could further damage teacher morale at a time when Fiji was already struggling to retain experienced teachers.

“The FTU had consistently raised concerns about the loss of about 730 teachers annually and the increasing attraction of overseas employment.

“When teachers are working in schools but then have their salaries stopped because of administrative or documentation problems, it creates insecurity and reinforces the perception that the profession is not being sufficiently valued.”

Mr Goundar said the Government needed to address more than salaries.

“It needs to address the efficiency, fairness and reliability of the systems that support teachers.”

item.title: Court adjourns murder trial involving couple
item.description: THE trial of a Sigatoka couple accused of forcing an 18-year-old student to ingest a lethal chemical three years ago has been adjourned to tomorrow by the High Court in Lautoka Mohammed Naushad and Nazreen Nisha Khan appeared before High Court Judge Justice Riyaz Hamza this afternoon each facing a charge of murder stemming from the alleged incident at a house in Maro on 30 June.
item.content:encoded:
THE trial of a Sigatoka couple accused of forcing an 18-year-old student to ingest a lethal chemical three years ago has been adjourned to tomorrow by the High Court in Lautoka

Mohammed Naushad and Nazreen Nisha Khan appeared before High Court Judge Justice Riyaz Hamza this afternoon each facing a charge of murder stemming from the alleged incident at a house in Maro on 30 June.

Mr Naushad faces an additional charge of criminal intimidation.

Defence lawyer Iqbal Khan, representing the couple alongside Samuela Heritage, immediately pressed the court for transcript access regarding the initial police interviews.

Justice Hamza said an application detailing this request would have to be made.

State lawyer Sheenal Swastika informed the court that while the state maintains a total list of 29 witnesses, prosecutors likely will not call every individual to the stand.

Instead, the state intends to notify defence counsel which specific witnesses will tender their official statements.

Justice Hamza adjourned the matter to tomorrow where it will be heard at 10am.

item.title: Teachers await pay | FTU demands salary restoration timeline
item.description: THE Ministry of Education has yet to give the Fiji Teachers Union a firm timeline for restoring the salaries of 134 teachers whose employment is being verified. FTU general secretary Muniappa Goundar told this newspaper yesterday the union expected payment to resume as soon as each affected teacher’s employment, appointment and documentation had been verified.
item.content:encoded:
THE Ministry of Education has yet to give the Fiji Teachers Union a firm timeline for restoring the salaries of 134 teachers whose employment is being verified.

FTU general secretary Muniappa Goundar told this newspaper yesterday the union expected payment to resume as soon as each affected teacher’s employment, appointment and documentation had been verified.

He said teachers should also receive all salary arrears properly due to them.

“We will continue pressing the ministry for a clear and specific timeframe rather than allowing legitimate teachers to remain unpaid indefinitely,” Mr Goundar said.

The union’s call comes as questions mount over the ministry’s payroll controls following Education Minister Aseri Radrodro’s disclosure that 13 “ghost employees” had remained on the payroll without being flagged earlier.

Mr Goundar said the ministry needed to explain how an employee whose contract had expired was able to remain on the payroll and receive salary payments until pay 18/2026.

“This is precisely the question that needs to be answered,” he said.

Mr Goundar said the FTU supported the ministry’s efforts to verify its payroll and prevent public funds from being improperly paid.

However, he said the situation raised concerns about the effectiveness of the ministry’s human resources, payroll and verification systems.

He said the concerns were heightened because the verification exercise followed recommendations in the Auditor-General’s 2024 report.

“The ministry needs to explain what controls were previously in place and why these discrepancies were not detected earlier.”

The FTU is now pressing for a clear timeframe for the restoration of salaries to verified teachers and payment of outstanding arrears.
